utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. May we have the appearances for today, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. On behalf of the Prosecution, I'm Tom Hannis, along with Alexis Demirdjian, and Jasmina Bosnjakovic our Case Manager.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, Your Honour. For Mr. Stanisic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Tatjana Savic, appearing for Stanisic Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: For Zupljanin Defence, Igor Pantelic and Dragan Krgovic appearing today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: On the 18th February, 2010, the Prosecutor -- Prosecution filed a motion seeking leave, inter alia, to add 98 new documents to its Rule 65 ter exhibit list. The Defence of both accused opposed to the motion in this respect. On the 22nd of February, the Prosecution informed the parties and the Chamber by e-mail that it intends to use 23 of these documents with Witness ST-166, who is about to take the stand. The Trial Chamber will now rule on the motion in respect with these 22 documents. Trial Chamber recalls that all documents on which Prosecution seeks to rely -- to rely to prove its case must be on the Rule 65 ter exhibit list. Amendments to the 65 ter exhibit list may be granted when the interests of justice allow. Factors to be taken into consideration include good cause, due diligence, lack of undue prejudice to the Defence and judicial economy. The Prosecution groups the 22 documents in two categories. First, 21 documents related to communication within the RS MUP, Rule 65 ter number 03500 to 03520. And, secondly, two recently received or re-evaluated documents, Rule 65 ter numbers 03557 and 03559. The Prosecution seeks the addition of the first category of documents, as a result of failure of the parties to reach agreement on the issue of communication within RS MUP. According to the Prosecution, these documents were disclosed to the Defence in September 2009. The Defence claims that this is an issue in dispute since 2007, and that the motion comes six months after the Defence refused to stipulate to communications. Moreover, only five of these documents pertain to municipalities of concern to the indictment and similar documents already exists -- exist on the Rule 65 ter list exhibit list. The Trial Chamber notes that one of these documents, document with Rule 65 ter number 03507, in this category has already been admitted into evidence as P395. With regard to the second category, the Prosecution does not provide any particular details about whether the two documents in question were recently received or whether they were re-evaluated, and if so, which reasons. Furthermore, the Prosecution does not provide any specific information as to when the documents were disclosed to the Defence. The Trial Chamber concludes that the Prosecution has neither shown good cause nor due diligence to justify, less than one week before the testimony of ST-166, the addition of these 23 documents to its Rule 65 ter exhibit list. Trial Chamber is not satisfied that the potential value of the -- to be attributed to these documents is such that would outweigh the prejudice that the Defence will suffer, should the request be granted. Given the fact that ST-166 is to begin testifying today, the Trial Chamber cannot see that it would be in the interests of judicial economy to postpone his testimony to allow the Defence adequate time to prepare. The motion is therefore denied in respect the 23 documents, and the Trial Chamber remains seized of the motion in all other respects.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Delvoie. Mr. Hannis, we have been alerted that you have a preliminary matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And it actually relates to the oral decision just granted. You may have noticed I came down to court yesterday afternoon near the end of the extended sitting because I was advised that there would perhaps be a ruling at that time. And I wanted to address some matters to your attention. Now that the decision has been made, I do want to put something on the record and perhaps try and persuade you to reconsider at least as to four of the documents. Not all 23. Part of what I was going to say yesterday afternoon was that, upon further review and having proofed the upcoming witness concerning those documents, I had decided that I only wanted to use four of the year-end reports, and later in the day upon learning that one, the one from Sanski Most, 03507, was already in evidence through Witness ST-161, back in November. I only had three. And those are for municipalities that are there in the indictment, Prijedor, which is document 3517; Teslic, as 65 ter 3519; and Kljuc, which is 65 ter 320. Regarding 3557, I was going to withdraw that document as well. But I did want to make an argument for 3559. All four of these documents do have some special pertinence to the continuing to be contested issue of communications. I know the Defence response included the argument that this has been an issue known to the Prosecution for two years. That's is certainly true as to Mr. Stanisic. Not to Mr. Zupljanin. He hasn't been here that long, for one thing. And most of these document are more pertinent to communications between Mr. Zupljanin's CSB and subordinate units and his units up. They don't pertain as directly to Mr. Stanisic as they do to Mr. Zupljanin. And the reason that these remaining three communications year-end reports have some special significance with this witness is that they are direct responses to a dispatch that he sent requesting that information. In his position as chief of the communications encryptographic data protection unit in the CSB.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't know that until I was proofing him earlier this week, and he -- his name is not in the document. His identification is related to the transmission number for the dispatch requesting the information, and he will tell you that his designator is something like 11-1/04. It's a particular identifier for him as the chief of the communications unit. And can you see that on -- on the Kljuc document as well as in the Sanski Most document. We do have other information about communications, Your Honour, but we don't think the issue is fully resolved. We have the draft MUP annual report which has some total numbers for communications made. We have in evidence a six-month report concerning communications from the Banja Luka CSB and a report for the three-month period between July and September. However, we think it is important to establish what communications were made to and from these three indictment municipalities. You have described in your oral ruling, Judge Delvoie, some of the factors that should be considered by the Trial Chamber in deciding whether or not to permit the late addition of evidence like this. We would urge you to consider that, absent a showing of intentional misconduct or bad faith or malice on the part of the Prosecution, or on any party, if it were later in this case, the ultimate sanction of barring the evidence shouldn't be imposed, if there is an alternative remedy. And since I'm now only asking for the three of the communication documents, not 21, we think the adequate remedy would be to allow some extra time. And I don't know how much time would be necessary to deal with this issue. These are not terribly complicated documents. They list the communication equipment held by each of these SJBs, the number of the communications they sent, and the state and functioning of those communications during the relevant time-period. So, with that, I just want to make an argument and request that you reconsider that possibility. And because this witness is uniquely placed to address them because he is the one who send the request out asking for the information to be received. If I can't address it with him, I don't know a witness later in the case that I could introduce it through. With regard to 3559, I can't tell, Your Honour, I think that's a document we had a long time. I'm not sure when it was re-evaluated and consider to be added. There is a communications aspect to that document as well, as there's a notation at the bottom of that message indicating that this report had been conveyed by telephone, as opposed to the usual means of transmitting such information, and again, we think that is important to show the alternative means of communication that were available in situations where the normal teletype equipment wasn't working. I guess that's all I had to say on the point. My other point was I -- I guess -- I was disappointed when I learned this morning at 10.30 that the decision was going be announced was not favourable to the Prosecution, and I -- I guess I suffered from my -- as a consequence of my usual optimism, the fact that I had not heard anything since last night, I thought perhaps the ruling was going in my favour. And if it was bad news, I would have changed my organisation and presentation for this next witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, the fact that the ruling that the Chamber has given an oral ruling doesn't mean that it isn't a considered ruling. And one of the reasons which you would have heard in Judge Delvoie's -- when he delivered the ruling was that the Prosecution had not shown good cause, so it is hardly of assistance if after the Chamber has ruled that you seek to advance reasons which one would have expected at the time the motion was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but some of the reasons - and I have just advanced - I did not become aware of until I was proofing this witness yesterday. Particularly his identity as the person who had requested this information. And there was no way could I know that before. His name does not appear in the documents; there's a numerical code. I wouldn't have known that if I hadn't asked about that in the course of proofing him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is there a response from the other side?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Briefly, Your Honour. We say the standard for reconsideration is the following. You may reconsider your discussion if there is -- the existence of a clear error of reasoning has been demonstrated. We say none has. Or if reconsideration is necessary in order to prevent an injustice. And again, as you have quite rightly have pointed out, Your Honour, your oral decision weighed the factors of prejudice to the accused, and you have made that ruling. And there is no argument been made to show that you were wrong on that. As for the first -- the only opportunity to interview this witness, that clearly can't be the case, since as we have been saying for the last three years - not two, three years now - since the interview with Mr. Stanisic, the Prosecution has been aware that it is a matter in dispute. So they could have had their investigators any time in the last two or three years meet with this or any other witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regards the position of Zupljanin Defence, we fully support what our colleague Mr. O'Sullivan has said. Our standpoint as regard communication has been known to the Prosecutor since August at least, when we challenged the issue of communication lines, so the OTP had time to interview the witness and include exhibits on their list. Any further reconsideration of this decision would be prejudicial to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, the Chamber is not unmindful of the plank in your arguments, that you have only become aware of the connection between the witness and these proposed three documents, having proofed the witness upon his arrival in The Hague. Nevertheless, inasmuch as the intimation by e-mail to the parties of the intended ruling of the Chamber would have only gone out about midday today, the Chamber is of the view that having become aware of this, it is something that one would have thought the Prosecution would have taken steps at some point, having become aware of this, to deal with their motion. And, therefore, the Chamber does not intend to re-call the order it has given, and that order stands. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I ask a question about that. Your position is that -- that when I became aware of what the ruling was going to be, I should have taken some step? When I -- I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: No. I may have misspoken.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I will attempt to rephrase it. Having become aware of -- having proofed the witness, but before you would have received intimation of the Chamber's ruling, there would, in the Chamber's view, have been time for you to approach the Chamber again by way of an amended motion or whatever to indicate this new fact. Which would have been absent, as you would have said, because you simply didn't know, in the original motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't want to inundate the Trial Chamber with needless paper. We had a motion pending. I guess I could have filed an amended motion to add to the additional information that I learned yesterday afternoon, but I was more focussed on trying to organise my examination of all of the remaining documents so I could complete him within the three hours of my time that I have allotted. And I would only say I understand -- I understand the Trial Chamber's decisions, but I think undue weight has been given to the allegation of prejudice to the Defence. I'm only asking for three communication documents, three reports. I don't think there has been a showing of great prejudice. I don't think the extreme remedy of denying the evidence is necessary -- I'll shut up. I know you've ruled. I'm ready to call the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Witness. Can we -- can we have your name, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Drago Rakovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And what is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 10th of September, 1951.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And what is -- what is your ethnicity, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And your profession.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An electrical engineer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this the first time you testify before this Tribunal or any Tribunal in -- on any matters, any Tribunal in your home country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time I have testified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then, Mr. Rakovic, this is how the proceedings will go on here. You are a Prosecution witness. That means that the Prosecution will first have some questions for you. After that, both Defence teams can, as well, put questions to you. There will be re-examination eventually from Prosecution after that. And, at the end, eventually, the Judges could have some questions for you as well. We sit in sessions from -- for -- from more or less 90 minutes with every time a break of 20 minutes after one hour and a half. We sit from 9.00 to quarter to 2.00, more or less. Or as today in the afternoon, from 2.15 to 7.00. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Concerning your appearance as a witness here, I understand when you were contacted by the OTP about coming to testify, you didn't volunteer. You didn't want to come. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you -- you came because you learned that if you -- you refused, the Prosecution could request a subpoena from the Court, ordering you to come.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that you are an electrical engineer by occupation. Are you currently employed; and, if so, where are you working now?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm currently working in same workplace as before. Head of the communications section. Earlier it was the section of communications and encryption.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in what organisation do you hold that position?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: Public security centre. It used to be the Security Services Centre in Banja Luka, Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us a little bit about your training to become an electrical engineer. Where did you go to school and when?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: I can. I finished primary school in my village of Sljiva near Banja Luka. In fact I started school there, and I continued my primary school eight years in Banja Luka and finished high school in Banja Luka too. That's where I studied electrical engineering in the university in 1977. From 1977 to 1978, I served in the JNA, my compulsory military service, after which, I found employment in the factory called Rudi Cajavac, and that's where I worked until 31st March, 1992, and then on 1st of April, 1992, I took a job in the Security Services Centre of the MUP. It was still the MUP of the B and H.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you tell the Judges a little bit about what the Rudi Cajavac enterprise was, what kind of work was done there, and, in particular, what was your job?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: Rudi Cajavac was a big conglomerate employing about 10.000 workers. It had three main work organisations and two auxiliary ones. One was the organisation of professional electronics where I worked. There was one enterprise producing car equipment. One factory producing TV sets, radios, and similar. And there were another two units one of which produced switches for washing machines and such. The last two were smaller units. They all comprised Rudi Cajavac. I worked in professional electronics. We called it military industry. I worked with measuring and detection devices, based on radio isotopes and chemical poisons. I worked there for 14 years, with one stint in research and development. It was called Independent Designer. For a while, I worked in the technology of preparation for production, and then some four or five years, I worked as chief of the production section in this unit, supervising around 700 to 800 workers. That was until 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. In 1991 and 1992, were you a member or active in any political party; and, if so, which one?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was. I was a member of the Serbian Democratic Party from the very first day, when it was founded.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us how, after working at Rudi Cajavac for 14 years, did you come to have a post with the MUP. How did you get a job at the police department?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know how it was. There were multi-party elections, you know, and positions in power were divided between the parties, and within political parties, people agreed who would work where. In many companies, including the one where I worked, we could feel there was a shortage of work, and I thought it would be a good idea to find a new job. It was not originally my idea to go to that sort of work, but it so happened that I was on sick-leave for a while, in hospital. I wasn't very active in the party either. People from my local commune, from my neighbourhood and community thought it would be a good idea to nominate me to the ministry, to the Security Services Centre, because I was an honest man and could be useful, both to the party and the people whom I would represent. That's what they thought. My first idea was to find employment in the postal services company where the salaries were and still are much better. But unfortunately wasn't around when these posts were being filled.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who -- who recommended you for a post in the MUP? Do you know by name, or affiliation with a political party?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: I had recommendations from my political party, my neighbours and people from my local commune. People who worked together with me who were activists, one of them was Momo Blajic, a good friend of mine. Vojo Jugovic, and late Miro Kraljevic. Those were people from my local commune who nominated me and recommended me. As far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. What was your job title or -- and your duties when you started with the CSB in Banja Luka on April 1st, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: My post was called chief of section for communications and encryption, as far as I remember. And my duties were -- in fact, the unit consisted of two sections. One section dealing with the maintenance of the existing equipment and machines, and another section dealing with the transfer of non-speech information, although this unit also contained the switchboard of the centre, and the encryption of messages. That's why it was called section for exploitation, in other words, encryption and data transfer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately how many people worked for you in the centre?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: In the centre, in the base itself, the unit that I headed had, to the best of my recollection, around 20 employees. Out of these 20, there were three supervisors, myself and another two unit supervisors, one of whom was systems engineer, that's how it was called. There were five or six workers dealing with maintenance. And around ten workers, some of them working on the switchboard, and around five of them were operators. And we had a special acronym for them because in the afternoons when the lady who worked the switchboard was away, they also served as telephone operators.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you have any employees under you who worked outside the centre, or is that the sum total of people that were under your supervision?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I was about to say. Outside the centre, across police stations, a certain number of our men also worked. The number depended on the size of the station, and it varied from one person to a team of five or six. The greatest number was in Prijedor, where we even had one chief of unit, one engineer, one technician, working on maintenance, and I believe six radio telegraph operators and encryptors. I'm talking about the situation as it was when arrived. In Jajce also we had a larger number. In other police stations, we had smaller numbers, except Bosanska Gradiska which had five or six, one of them for maintenance and around five were radio telegraph operators and encryptors. Other stations had about two people. My competence was, so to speak, line competence, meaning professional work. In terms of their official status, they were attached to these people to the corresponding public security station, so that I supervised only the technical part of the work and perhaps hiring.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I next want to ask you about the means of communication that were available in CSB Banja Luka in 1992, after you started working there. And, first of all, for voice communication, what were the means available to communicate by voice within CSB Banja Luka in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: There was a number of communications. When you say "voice communication," that means primarily telephone traffic. Other means were not used much, at least at that time. It was called the so-called KT traffic but also voice communication, UKT. Telephone traffic, one, two KT, and three UKT, and non-voice communication radio telegraph. That was the fourth.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How many -- how many phone lines were available to the outside world from the CSB in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: If I remember well, at the Security Services Centre there was a small number of what we call direct telephone lines. Those were mostly available to supervisors and chiefs. I was one of those who had a direct telephone line. There was several, perhaps three or four telephone lines, in the state security sector, and five or six in the public security sector. The chief had one telephone number, and the rest operated through the switchboard. Everyone who wanted to make calls would call the switchboard and most incoming calls would come to the switchboard of the Security Services Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And for those of you who had direct lines, you could make and receive calls without using the switchboard; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. As far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And to the best of your recollection, how were those direct outside phone lines working in Banja Luka in 1992? Could you communicate with Bijeljina, Pale?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot say how they communicated because I personally didn't communicate with anyone. That's why I don't know. I really can't talk about that. Whether communications were available or not, I can't say, because I had no need to call anyone, and I didn't call anyone. Whether the lines actually worked, whether they were breakdowns or not, I can't say with any certainty. I know there were breakdowns, but how long and how often, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who would have been responsible for the maintenance of telephone lines when they broke down? Would that be one of your two unit supervisors, the one for maintenance of equipment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, the most breakdowns were caused by breakdowns of communications at the PTT, the Postal Services Centre. And then you either had to call the PTT - I don't know what they were called later, telecom or whatever - but it was the section that was in charge directly of telephones. The chief of maintenance was an experienced person. He had worked there for a long time, and he knew exactly who to call. He was the one. Stipo Ojdenic [phoen] was his name. He would always call his own people with whom he had worked for 20 years back. He would say, We have a breakdown here, what are we going to do about it. We had another person dealing with other sort of maintenance Mustafa Hasanovic, an engineer. He even replaced the chief for a while. They would stand in for each other. As far as the maintenance of the switch board is concerned, Mile Sakic was in charge. I don't know if the name means anything to you. He was a Croat. He was the chief maintenance master for the switchboard, the telephone switchboard, but also the telegraph switchboard, which connected the teletype system.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If there had been severe problems with the phone lines, as the chief of communications, would you not have heard about it in some fashion? For example, seeing increased request for short-wave radios or other kinds of communication to make up for the shortage caused by problems with the phone lines?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: Clearly, I was informed. The people who worked in that section would came and say, Chief, we are in trouble. There's a breakdown there and there, and, of course, I was aware of these things. We would then talk and try to see if there's another way, an alternative. But if the problem arose in the system itself, and regardless of how old our equipment was we had a telephone switchboard that was installed in 1970. Therefore, it was 20 years old. We had a telephone switchboard OM 60 that was installed at the same time when the Security Services Centre was set up in that building. Also very, very old. But we had not much problems with that. The greatest problems arose at the post office. That's where the lines broke down. So our job, in that case would be to contact people from the post office, their maintenance section, and that's why I told you that we used our employees who had worked with the post office employees in those places for 20 years back, and sometimes we had other problems, such as power blackouts. It happened very often. Every now and then, there was no electricity. At one point in Banja Luka, we had no electricity for two months. Then we would have to use power generators. Then there were shortages of fuel. Problems were everywhere. It was not just in our station.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. What time-period are you talking about where there was no electricity for two months? When was that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war. It was -- I can't say exactly. It could have been in the second half of 1992. But I think it must have been in that initial period, in the first half of 1992. As far as I know, the territory was also cut in half. We couldn't pass through. The corridor was opened on the 28th of June. All the way until the 28th of June, you couldn't travel. And the main sources of electricity were near Brcko and the lines went from there towards Croatia and towards Krajina, and we in the Krajina, had great problems. Sometimes we would be able to provide electricity from this power plant, only to -- for the barest necessities. And I always tried with the electricity company to get priority for our centre, to get them to allocate to us a special line, but I can't tell you exactly whether it was in May or June, or sometime later, perhaps, but around that time, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In spite of these problems, based on our preparation for your testimony, it seemed as though teletype communications, dispatches, were occurring on a regular basis to and from the centre in Banja Luka. So you managed to get the power to run your teletype machine just about everyday, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you say that. But you couldn't say it was true of the entire territory. That is the point. We could get it to work for a short time, perhaps in Banja Luka, for instance. But it couldn't work in some other place, and we couldn't switch on the teletype communication in -- in whatever direction, when there was no electricity. You can't say we were able to work all the time. Yes, we did work all the time, but how? There was perhaps a possibility to work from two or three stations or to send to two or three stations, but not the fourth, and the fourth station would have to wait for two or three days until the problem was solved. The system worked. Our switchboard was plugged in; but the point was that I couldn't contact the person I wanted to contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the event that you weren't able to have communication by phone or teletype, did you sometimes use couriers to deliver messages?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: You know, in my service, when a dispatch comes in and we do whatever we are able to do with it, I have to tell you we didn't have a courier service in my section. If a courier service existed it was attached to the centre. We still have the registry office where mail is sent or delivered, and when somebody happens to travel they could take it with them. But in my section, we didn't have a courier service. I didn't have a messenger to whom I could give whatever I needed to send. We would sometimes return dispatches to the sender and what happened after that, I don't know. I can only make assumptions. But assumptions are no good to you, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, sometimes assumptions can be useful. When you were not able to send something that had been delivered to you for transmission and you returned it to the person who gave it to you, wouldn't it be logical that they would try to use a courier?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe it would be logical. My duty, our duty, stopped once we returned the dispatch. I don't know what happened next.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we leave this topic, I wanted to ask you about two other means of voice communication that you mentioned. You talked about KT and UKT. Can you explain for the Judges what those two things are and how they differ, one from another?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: Here's the thing. The UKT system is the traditional system used by the police, the operative police. The UKT system was relatively well preserved, in the sense that the main repeaters on Mount Kozara were working. It was operational. So with mobile patrols, we could, from Novi Grad and the Banja Luka municipality, use that. In individual police stations, there were local repeaters. They were also preserved. However, the problem with a part of the UKT was that we didn't have an adequate number of devices. Our devices were already obsolete and this part of the factory at Rudi Cajavac, the section that produced TV sets and radios, did not have enough raw materials, and their production nearly stopped in 1991/1992. Supply ran dry. And UKT is the traditional traffic for operative police. I can see it here and everywhere. Not much new has been invented in that sense. It was not scrambled -- KT [as interpreted], I mean. KT was not scrambled. Anyone could switch into it. Our people who came back to our country from abroad started bringing all sorts of ham radios, and everyone could get involved in this KT traffic. As for UKK traffic, that was a short-wave system. In our system, at that time, it wasn't used for regular traffic. We just did occasional checks to see if the system was working. I know that in some tactical exercises the police used these KT devices and within this KT system we had two mobile communications centres, RTU 100 and RTU another one in Prijedor, but that didn't mean much in terms of communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... to my friend. I think it a page 21, line 24, witness said it was not scrambled KT, I mean, I believe I heard that witness mentioned UKT. So please, Mr. Hannis, if you can clarify that with the witness just for the accuracy of the transcript because obviously there are difference between KT and UKT. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I think the rest of his answer makes it clear, but I'll ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, what was scrambled? Was it KT traffic or UKT?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: What I said was that UKT was the operative system. We did not have any stations with scramblers. So anyone who had a UKT station could join in the traffic. They would just tune into the frequency, and they would join in. There was no way you could exclude them. There was no way you could tell who was jamming the line or hindering communication, which is why I said that the UKT system was not set up properly, and it still hasn't been set up properly. There is no money now again, so it was never set up properly, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What does the abbreviation UKT stand for, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: Ultra short-waves.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And KT stands for short-wave?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Short-wave.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was short-wave traffic scrambled? Did you have scramblers to do that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. It was open traffic. It was used by ham radio operators, amateur radio operators use that system frequently. There was no protection, and it wasn't really used in police work, to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So then for UKT that was your primary means of radio communication within the MUP, is that correct, voice communication by radio?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: The operative police, the police stations, that is public security stations, mostly used UKT traffic for police work. For regular police work, these were mobile patrols, patrols on foot. Any police station had a stationary radio station. That's why I say that this was the system that was mostly used by the police. Those who sat in offices used telephones, but the police were not sitting in offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was the approximate effective range of those units for UKT?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: That depends on how it was set up, if there was a stationary station with large watt output. Ours were mainly 25 watts. But there was a repeater on Mount Kozara, so if the station was operating in duplex or semi-duplex, that is, you would have a station and repeater and another station, then the range, because these waves travel in a straight line, so they could go as far as 80 kilometres. So if you had a station on Mount Kozara and there was a patrol which had a station, a mobile station in their car, of some 20 watts or so, they could communicate by means of the repeater on Mount Kozara to a distance of some 70 kilometres. It would depend on their position. As for the UKT stations operating in simplex, that would actually be only a few kilometres provided there was no wall or obstruction intervening, so these handheld radio stations were used, for example, on football stadiums, they could communicate across the football stadium, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let's talk now about written documents and how they were communicated. First of all, can you tells what the term "dispatch" means to you in the MUP, in the communications section. What is a "dispatch?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: A dispatch is, in actual fact, a telegram. That's how we used the word. Sometimes we even used the word "telegram." I found forms saying telegram form, rather than dispatch form. A dispatch should be brief, clear, it should contain a message or information up to a certain number of words in A-5 format. Anything exceeding A-5 format, which is half of A-4, would no longer be a dispatch; it would be some other sort of material, an instruction or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how were they created in your centre? What equipment did you have?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: In our centre we didn't write dispatches. We retyped them and sent them. It was the senders who wrote them. They created the dispatches. And they were typed in their offices or services. We would take the typed dispatches over. They would be taken to the room from which dispatches were sent. It would be re-typed on the teleprinter and sent to the addressees mentioned on the form. And when that had been done, when it had been sent or not sent, because sometimes it couldn't be sent to all the addresses, then the dispatch, the original dispatch, should be sent back to the sender, and if there were some addresses where we had not been able to send it, we would note that on the dispatch, saying that we couldn't send it to such and such an address.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Help me a little on the process. If I'm the chief in your centre and I want to send a dispatch, I, or my secretary, type it up, is it signed before you receive it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: According to the rules, dispatches were supposed to be signed by the sender. There was more than one sender in the security service. There wasn't just one person who would send dispatches. It could come from two different sectors, two different services, and we lower-ranking officers who are in charge of smaller units were able to write and sign dispatches. As a rule, they would arrive with the signature of the sender. Very often it would happen that a dispatch would arrive with a signature, but it would have a heading and, underneath, there would be the first and last name of the person in whose name it was being sent; but the sender would put a comma and sign their name. It would be someone else. For example, I would know if I was sending a dispatch to an external organ, a company, for example, because it was my duty to contact with the post office, with the electric power supplier, and so on, and then I would put the heading there. If I thought that the centre of the service is one organisational unit, and I was authorised to do their job on behalf of the whole unit, I couldn't put my heading there and my name and then write on behalf of the whole centre, because then I would be using the centre's heading. I would write the dispatch, and I would put the name of the head of the centre, and then I would put a comma, because I was authorised, and then I would sign my name. I would stamp this with the stamp of the centre. I would enter the number of the centre, and then send it. And a dispatch of that kind couldn't emanate my service on behalf of the centre. It had to be sent as a centre dispatch, so to say, so that I saw some dispatches -- I never actually looked at the other dispatches. I only looked at the ones that I had written, and it was the operatives who took over the dispatches and retyped them and entered them into the log-books who would read them, actually. I never read anybody else's dispatches.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: According to the rules, I take it from your last answer, then, that only certain persons were authorised to send -- or to author dispatches for sending; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's right. For example a subordinate of mine could not send a dispatch on behalf of my department, so that there were lines work, you see. And, of course, people dealing with the uniformed police, for example, could send a dispatch on behalf of their service. Those on behalf -- or, rather, they could send dispatches on behalf of the centre. So it's correct that the stations on the ground, for example, had certain rights and work they could do. No one, especially determined this, but it is something we inherited and something that was common knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in CSB Banja Luka, where were you and your unit or your section physically located? Were you all together in one portion of the building?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: My unit was on the third floor. When you go upstairs, it was in the left -- or, rather, in the right wing. Half of the third floor was my unit. We all sat there together. We even had a door through which one entered our unit with a little window for the delivery of dispatches, and there was a bell you could ring, and there was a code for employees so they could enter, just as you have badges do enter certain parts of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So I take it there was limited access to your area. Who was allowed in, other than you and your subordinate workers? Anyone else have the code and access to your area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: In the area where I was sitting and where maintenance was, various people could enter there. Somebody would ring the bell, be admitted, bring in a station and wait around for it to be repaired. People would come to see us on business, and so on. But there was this other area where dispatches were sent. That was the unit for cryptographic protection for encryption and so on. And there, unauthorised persons could not enter. Only the personnel actually working there could go there. The chief, the operator, the switchboard operator, there were several officers there. There was one where there was a teleprinter, another with Faraday's Cage where we encrypted and decrypted dispatches or decoded dispatches, and no one else could enter that area. Well, maybe if somebody reported to me and then we went there together to take a look or the republican inspector arrived to inspect the documents for cryptographic protection and so on. But if someone entered without authorisation, under the old rules, which I then thought were the normal rules, in the centre, the centre would be locked up until the -- all the premises were looked at to make sure that nothing untoward had happened. This never happened while I was there, but that's what I heard happened before. For example, a republican inspector could arrive and say that work was prohibited until certain things were -- had been checked, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How about Chief Zupljanin? Did he have access to any or all of your communications section?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: Nowhere did it say he didn't have access. But, as far as I know, he never came there. Whether he dropped in, in the afternoon I really couldn't say. But most probably, no one would have prevented him, as the chief, from entering, or any other chief. The chief could enter. The personnel working there could enter. I or the chief of communications could enter. The republican inspector could enter. And they would bring in colleagues sometimes. They were considered to be persons under oath, persons who were duty-bound to preserve the confidentiality of the encryption system. And when people retired, for a year or two afterwards they still had to keep confidential information secret and not divulge anything. So if the chief had dropped in and said to me, Rakovic, can I look around and see what is going on? Of course, I would have let him. Or he might have done that in the afternoon and said hello to someone. Well, probably yes. Well, the cleaners would go in as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me stop you there. You mentioned encryption. I take it there were certain kinds of written communications that needed to be more confidential than others. And those were encrypted before being sent out? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I take it that there were certain written communications that were not sent open text, that they had to be encrypted or encoded before being sent out of your centre; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: If it said "encrypted," then it had to be encrypted. If there was a sign saying that it is to be encrypted, then that's what had to be done. If there was a letter S, with a diacritic, that is, that meant it had to be encrypted. It was obligatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who made that decision? Was that you in the communications centre or the author or someone else?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge there were certain instructions. When I arrived there, the instructions were already in place. Every dispatch that was send -- well, it was the sender who thought about whether it should be encrypted or not. If it arrived from a higher level, for example, I would get a dispatch from a higher level which said it had to be encrypted, then I had to collect certain information, and I was passing it on, I would have to send it as an encrypted dispatch, and they would have to send it back as encrypted. So I couldn't say, Well, the guy higher up said it had to be encrypted, and I'm not going to encrypt it. That was not something one would do if one was working according to regulations, but what happened in actual fact, well, the rules may not always have been respected. Some people may have broken the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you ever see the reverse situation where you given something that was not for encryption, but upon looking at it, you realized that maybe it should be? Did that ever happen?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: Sometimes staff members would come to see me, and they would say, Chief -- these were experienced staff members. They would say, Chief, look at this. This should be encrypted. And then we would send a note saying we thought this had to be encrypted. Because, of course, you know, there were multi-party -- there was a multi-party system, new people arrived. They didn't even know what a dispatch was. Security station would get a new chief, and they wouldn't know. There was no way he could find out that something should not be sent as open text, and then, most probably, such things did happen. And on my part, I may have warned people on the ground. I think I even sent a dispatch to that effect, saying that such things should not happen. And I informed the chiefs of the public security stations. I think I sent out a message of that sort after all those warnings and employees coming to tell me that this was not something that should be done like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you about the actual physical act of encrypting a message. Can you tell us briefly in the simplest layman's terms or non-engineer terms, that you can, how that was done, in your centre?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Mr. Hannis, I don't know long this answer is going to be, but although we are a minute shy of the ordinary time for taking a break, it may be convenient to take the break now, and then --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I suspect it may be a longer answer, so time -- now would be a good time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, while we're waiting for the witness, I shouldn't conceal my curiosity as to how the question of encryption is relevant to the case, but I'm sure you will enlighten us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think some of these that we have been talking about are things that are probably fairly common knowledge most of us here, but absent judicial notice, I think it is necessary for me to put some things in the record. I will try to keep it brief. I take your point.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Rakovic, I have been alerted that sometimes the interpreters are having a hard time keeping up with you when you're giving some of your longer answers, because you are speaking quickly, which is understandable. But I have been asked to request that you try and slow your answers down about a bit. Thank you. When we broke, I wanted to ask you to explain briefly, if you could, in layman's terms as best as possible, how a dispatch was encrypted when it was received in your unit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: The operator who is sending dispatches would take over the dispatch, look at it, and see that it was encrypted marked S with a diacritic, Sh. He takes it to the so-called cage which contained all the equipment, the tele-type and the encryption and decryption machines. He would go into the cage, re-type the dispatch. First he would type out the text from the dispatch, and then this re-type was on a tape, on a roll that would -- he would install on the encryption machine, and the encryption machine turned the text into code, into symbols. And it would sent it to destination; that's the point of encryption. At destination the same procedure runs vice versa. The receiving employee sees that he has receiving encrypted, puts it into the decryption machine, and it comes out as normal text. Like we would do when we received encrypted material. I never personally did this work. I never entered this cage to see how it was done, but I know what a teletype is; it is basically a type writer with some additional accessories. I saw how it works, but I never actually did it myself. I didn't go into that cage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Part of the process when -- when the operator has typed in the message that needs to be encrypted, what happens to the original message that he was working from, the one that had been signed by the author and delivered to your unit? What becomes of that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: The initial message, either encrypted or not, was returned to the sender. The person who brought the message in the first place would come to recover it, or sometimes the signalsman would go and return it himself when nobody came for it. Whoever sent the message would put some sort of sign or initial to indicate it was sent, and then it was returned to the sender. All the dispatches looked the same. It's ordinary letters and everything, except when it is marked Sh, S with a diacritic, it means that it had been encrypted before sending. So that nobody between our end and the other end could sort of intercept it and see it as it was. They couldn't decrypt it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So in addition to the operator putting his initials or some mark on the copy that is returned to the author after the dispatch has been sent, did you within your unit keep some kind of record of dispatches that you have sent and dispatches that have you received?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: In our organisational unit, the section for transmission, we had log-books. I believe we had at least four. At this moment I have 25 log-books, for instance. We, as the centre, with lots of incoming and outcoming messages, had four log-books. Two log-books recorded incoming dispatches; one book was for open dispatches, and the other one for coded. And two log-books were for outgoing messages, both open and encrypted. Sometimes when we would need it to run checks, when somebody wanted to check if something was really sent or received, et cetera, we would be able to trace it in the log-book because we would enter in the log-book various codes. SJB, for instance, stood for a police station or PS, we would know who the receiving party was. And accordingly, we would log in all the open messages and encrypted messages in outgoing mail log-books. And thanks to these books we could prove, if somebody was claims otherwise, that we have or have not received something or have or have not sent something. In smaller stations they had fewer log-books. First of all, there was a shortage and, in any case there were maximum two log-books. One for incoming, one for outgoing. And the incoming then would contain both open and encrypted. As far as I remember, encrypted messages accounted for 5 to 10 per cent of the overall, whereas as all the others were open, 90 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to show you a document now. This is 65 ter number 2402. And it's a long document. The first page will be up on your screen in just a second. And I'll ask you if you can recognise it. Do you recall having looked at this before testifying today?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: I looked at these books in the course of proofing and interviews. I just can't remember whether this is the precise book I've seen, judging by the dates. It says: Received open, from 27 November 1992 to 2nd August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. If we could go to page 3 in both the English and the B/C/S. Could you take a look at that, and by looking at the headings and the various entries under those headings, can -- can you tell us anything further about what this is a log-book of.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: You can see, looking at this page, B 0071010, that dispatches were logged here as they came in. So they are received dispatches. One column indicates from whom, Grahovo, Teslic, Mrkonjic Grad, Bihac, Prijedor, MUP Teslic, Srbac, Laktasi. This is in the "from" column. The next column is "to." It's mainly full of CSB, CSB. All I can see is this is a log-book of received dispatches. I can see from whom they arrived, and I know for whom they were intended, CSB, but I don't know if they were to be sent on somewhere else. I can see in one of the lines, 29 November, marked that there is an indication, operations duty service. I can't see much more. We can see from whom they arrived and for whom they were intended. It is mainly CSBs, the addressee.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] On the far right of the document, I think it's being scrolled over now for you to see. There are what appear to be initials or signatures. Is that how it was normally done?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: It's the signature of the person who received it. I think it was signed by operators, radio telegraph operators. They would initial as a sign that they received it. You see this bracket encompassing several lines and then he would sign next to it. Another thing could be, is that this is the signature of the person who recovered the dispatch, when the operator gives the dispatch to the person for whom it was intended, such as someone in the CSB. And then he would call somebody, like a secretary, and the secretary would then come, and perhaps it's the secretary who signed to indicate that she took the dispatch and physically took it to -- to whomever.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender this document. I would indicate that it goes beyond the 31st of December, 1992, but I would suggest that we should have the whole document in now. I think it will link up with other evidence to come in the case and some that has already been in. It will assist us perhaps in tracking certain documents as to when they were received in Banja Luka, and that may carry significance later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Exhibit P1001, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My apologies. It's been too long since I moved to tender a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, next I'd like to show you a document that is in evidence already, just to ask you a question about some markings on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it is P553.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this -- sorry. This is appears to be a dispatch or a telegram from your centre, addressed to various SJB chiefs and the President of certain Serbian municipalities. Can you tell us what this is? Can you recognise this by the format and the typing?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: Looking at this document, it's marked 0043264, I see the heading: Security Services Centre Banja Luka, dispatch number 11-115. And then it says: SJB - everybody - and then many places, because I don't know why it's written like this, because when you say "for everybody," then you don't indicate all of them by name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: And, at the bottom, I believe it is the chief of the centre who signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there and ask a couple specific questions. Do you recognise this typewritten format as being distinctive of a teletype, or a telegram?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you show me the bottom, the signature? Well, just from looking at it, it's a classic dispatch. It has a header, indication of addressees, text, and signature. It looks like it was transmitted by teletype, whether it could indeed be sent to teletype to all of these entities. When I see written "president of the Serbian municipalities," and then I see which municipalities, we did not have teletype communication with all of them. So it doesn't really fit. I don't see how it could have worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you a couple of specific questions. At the top, where it has CSB, Banja Luka, there's a dispatch number 11-115. Can you tell us what the 11 signifies? What does that refer to in a dispatch from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were all sorts of numbers. I suppose this number was a reference to our centre. It says Security Services Centre, Banja Luka, dispatch number 11. There are no additions, if we had something added, for instance, my service was "11-1/" and then the number of the dispatch. Looking at this, I suppose it went from the chief -- the chief, and I see the signature is also from the chief, and that that -- that's logical. Then we should look up this number in the log-book or notebook of the person who recorded dispatches at the chief's office, and we would find the same number in our log-book of messages transmitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Didn't all the dispatches sent from Banja Luka CSB begin with a number 11 in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: I think so. Can you see from here that it is the case. Because the other numbers would indicate another organisational unit. That's what I said. 11-1/01, was general police. We were/04. So this first number is the same for everyone. And then have you this other number that indicates the date and the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. We will have more dispatches to look at, and I think we will see some with those -1/01 or /04, et cetera, that you were just telling me about. Here, though, for -- the number is 11-115. What is the 115? Is that a sequential number. In other words, is that the 115th dispatch sent out by 11, CSB Banja Luka in 1992? Is that what that second number refers to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: This second number should be the number of the dispatch, the sequential number of the dispatch. That means that the previous number should have been 114. The next one should be 116. That's how it should be if it were sent from the same service.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I see typewritten to the right of that in quotation marks the letters "DX." Can you tell us what that is and what it stands for.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: DX indicates urgency. It's the third order of urgency, so it is not operationally urgent. The first order was very urgent; the next one was DD. It had to be sent back then within two hours, nowadays it would also have to be sent immediately. And DX was to be sent within four hours. All this has been changed by now. Then the next order would be within 16 hours. We can also see from this that it is an open dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me try and clarify that. How many levels of urgency were there, and what were the designators? First of all, what was the designation for the most urgent, and how quickly did that have to be sent?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: According to the rule book on dispatch transmission that I was familiar with, the levels were as follows: Very urgent. We had no such dispatches in our centre, at least I don't remember. Then the next level would be DD --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Wait, let me stop you. What would be the letter or abbreviation for that, even though you didn't see one in your --

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: It would be spelled like that, "very urgent."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me about the next level down.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: The next level down was DD. An urgent dispatch that would be transmitted within two hours, but it's been changed now, especially since we don't have any dispatches marked "very urgent." The DDs are sent practically immediately. DD is followed by DX. The level of urgency was four hours. The next down was D. Means eight hours, one work shift. And after D, followed O. That was operative urgency. It to be transmitted within 16 hours. So that dispatches created within one work shift would not be late. They would have to be transmitted in the next shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. And the last question on this document --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could scroll to the bottom of the page in both English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see the name Mirko -- and my translation says: Received by Mirko 30 April 1992 at 0942? Do you know anything about who that is and what that means on this document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it means it was received by Mirko. We had at that time a signalsman called Mirko Dentaric [phoen], and we can see when we received it at, 0942 hours. Fact he sent it at 0942; he didn't receive it. He sent it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me show you next 65 ter 00103.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, please, this you said this was exhibited as P553; right? You said that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes. And could you -- could you indicate where I can find it on your list to use with this witness? Perhaps your Case Manager could assist. Because I can't find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Do you have a 65 ter number?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have a 65 ter number, 00104.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I thought we sent you a --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, 104, I thought we sent you a list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yeah, I have it, okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's a consolidated list, which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yeah, but the P number isn't mentioned on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I know, but for ease of future reference, Your Honour, I think it's sorted in the chronological order. So this the 29th of April and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay, thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next, 00103, 65 ter. You see this one, then, Mr. Rakovic. Again, is this a dispatch that would have gone out from your centre in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: Can we just enlarge this writing a bit? This is fine. It's similar to the one before. The heading, the number, to whom it is sent. Everything is almost the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, in the last one, and this one as well, we see some handwriting on the top. Can you tell us anything about where that comes from and when it would have been put on?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this handwritten addition, I suppose, could only have been made by the recipient. That's what I think. Because the sender, if the sender had written this, we would have been unable to transmit it. We wouldn't know what to write. However, the recipient, one of these police stations or chiefs of police stations, they would, and I'd do the same thing, they would write something about what had to be done about the dispatch in longhand. Maybe he made copies, and it says something like it has to be sent to other police stations. And then I see initials. That means the person who received this dispatch made a note what had to be done, probably had it copied, because, as far as I know, these are police stations. They did not have the equipment. It could have been transmitted to them by fax or somehow. The rest is the same as in the previous dispatch, apart from the text, which I didn't read.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I think you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, it would indicate that the ERNs that begin with a P are from a Prijedor collection, and that is where this document came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is this a standard practice by the receiving party when you receive a dispatch to, perhaps, make some handwritten notations on it as to how it should be distributed or any remarks? Would you do that in your centre in Banja Luka when you received a dispatch?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can say that I did, for myself. Sometimes a dispatch would arrive addressed to someone, usually a high-ranking chief, and we would call the secretary who would probably write 01, 02, 03, 04, and so on. It says here to stations various stations, crime investigation service, police department, and so on and so forth. So it might happen, that would be the practice. When a dispatch arrived addressed to someone, something had to be written on it. When you sent me a request to come to testify here, if it arrived in my chief's office, he would have initialed it to show his approval and that he was aware of why I would be absent, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that one, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Exhibit P1002, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next, if we could show the witness 65 ter number 1469. This is dated the 13th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I suppose that all of this goes to showing the mode of communication from and to the various MUP departments, and in particular, the CSB in Banja Luka. I wonder if this is disputed and if it could be stipulated? What's the position of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you have anticipated my standpoint. The witness may describe the manner of communication and the form of the document, whereas, we are admitting the whole document including it's content, and the witness knows nothing about the content of the document. Those are my reservations. I do not object to the witness testifying about the forms of various documents, the manner of their sending. However, if a document is admitted into evidence and we also admit the contents of the document, there is always a danger that the we will admit a document that the witness knows nothing about as regards its content.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's not necessary, he doesn't have to know about the content. If it is authentic - and he's a person who can establish its authenticity because of his work - then the document comes in and speaks for itself. Other witnesses can come in and talk about the contents and say whether they are accurate true or false, but it's in. That's my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I did not rise when the first document was admitted because it was already in evidence in fact. But this second document was not an exhibit. It is my standpoint that perhaps Mr. Hannis should have used dispatches that had already been admitted into evidence so that this witness could describe the form, the manner of sending, and so on. Now there is a latent danger that a document might slip in that the witness can not comment upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: As far as I have understood, Mr. Cvijetic, this witness is testifying to the authenticity of these documents and -- and as I started out by saying, the gist that I get of this is the evidence of how communications were made between, as I said, the MUP departments, and here, in particular, to and from the CSB in Banja Luka, that, of course, is important evidence. But my question to you was whether -- whether this is at all in dispute, and if it is not, then we might as well just go ahead and admit these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I had to written -- I thought I copied Mr. Cvijetic, but I know I wrote Mr. Zecevic and Mr. Pantelic a couple of days ago indicating that with this witness, what I was primarily doing with most of the documents was simply trying to have them authenticate him, and I was not going to be asking him about content per se. I'm asking him about some of the markings, numbers and, you know, routing information and urgency, et cetera, because that is what he knows about. But not about the content itself. And I -- I ask, if they had a position about whether or not we could reach some agreement. Mr. Zecevic was sick and told me he would try get back to me, but I haven't heard. And if I need to do this way, I will do it this way. But it takes the witness and I a little longer than I hoped it would to go through them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if I may be of assistance. The position of Zupljanin Defence is the following, and of course along the lines that my learned friend Mr. Cvijetic just made his submission. First of all, yes, I agree with the Prosecution that this particular witness, Mr. Rakovic, is of primarily assistance to explain technical point of view with these communications. We don't have problem with that, absolutely. Mr. Rakovic is obviously [indiscernible] professional, of course. On the other hand, I think that Mr. Rakovic can speak only on behalf of himself and his department, and these particular number of dispatches can be admitted as exhibit through this particular evidence. The prudent and, I would say, fair way would be for the other dispatches, which I don't have any problem with Mr. Hannis to offer, should be marked for identification. And then, at certain stage with the relevant witness, Mr. Hannis can, or Defence can, tender it into evidence. Otherwise, Your Honour, as you -- I'm sure you follow this very detailed explanation ever Mr. Rakovic, the practice in CSB Banja Luka was the following. And Mr. Rakovic also did it in his work. He, himself, signed Stojan Zupljanin as a signatory in dispatch and sent it to telecom or the other public companies, et cetera. And then if we are looking at the particular dispatch, the author is Stojan Zupljanin, but in fact he isn't. The author is, in this particular case, Mr. Rakovic. He explained that in his previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that misstates his evidence. He didn't say he was the author of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, no, he said when -- when he said that on behalf of head of centre --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And perhaps we should have this discussion outside the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, no, I'm sorry, we can clarify that at a later stage. So basically, yes, we don't have --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. We should have this discussion outside of the presence of the witness. I don't want him tainted by something that I say or something that one of my learned friends says across the way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Rakovic, the usher would escort you out of -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic and Mr. Pantelic, on a purely practical level, inasmuch as in a trial we can only deal with witnesses sequentially and what from Mr. Hannis has said about the purpose of the identification, for want of a better word, of the -- of the documents through this witness, wouldn't it make -- wouldn't it be practical and convenient and cause no real harm to the Defence if they exhibited it, as Mr. Hannis proposes?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: First of all, yes, Your Honour, I will give my submission. It is a page 26, line 10, of today's transcript. This witness said the following: "I would write the dispatch, and I would put the name of the head of the centre, and then I would put a comma because I was authorised ..." et cetera. That was my particular submission with regard to the testimony of this witness, this -- this afternoon. Where -- I'm coming now to my previous submission. Where I don't have any particular problem that Mr. Hannis offers a number of these pages going from department where Mr. Rakovic was a head. I have any problem with that. That but I have a problem with the other number of dispatches where the name of my client is at the end of dispatch, and in accordance with the practice it was made by, I would say, public security or financial centre, et cetera, then we are loosing our track. And it is not fair. It is not in the interests of justice or my client to have these dispatches exhibited through this witness where, obviously, the practice was -- was very, very specific in CSB. So that's why I'm asking and kindly request that all other dispatches should be marked for identification. I don't know how many Mr. Hannis will offer. And that a limited number, where this particular witness can say, Yes, I was the author, Yes, I know this dispatch, I don't have any problem to be admitted.
